L29: # Russian earthquake causes minor disturbance in Devils Hole
L30:

The background is an underwater scene of brown sediment and two pillars of dark green algae. Screenshot of a video taken on July 30 shows pupfish swimming and reduced amounts of algae on the shallow shelf after the recent earthquake.

L35: News Release Date: July 31, 2025
L36: Contact: cite5†DEVA News L37: Contact: cite6†Abby Wines , 760-786-3221
L38: AMARGOSA VALLEY, Nev. – On July 29, just 21 minutes after a magnitude 8.8 cite7†earthquake†earthquake.usgs.gov struck Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, waves were triggered nearly 4,000 miles away in Death Valley National Park. Earthquakes can generate cite8†waves†en.wikipedia.org in enclosed bodies of water, even over surprising distances.
L39: cite9†Devils Hole†www.nps.gov is a water-filled cave approximately 12 feet wide and over 500 feet deep, with a water surface that is typically sheltered from wind and remains extremely calm. The endangered Devils Hole Pupfish depend on a shallow shelf at the cave’s mouth for most of their food and spawning.
L40: The pupfish's habitat was previously affected by earthquake waves in cite10†December†www.nps.gov and February, which removed most of algae and invertebrates that pupfish rely on for food. During the official survey in March, only cite11†38 fish†www.nps.gov were counted.
L41: Fortunately, biologists are less concerned about the impacts of the July 29 quake on the pupfish. The waves generated by this earthquake were smaller than those from the previous quakes, as the epicenter was farther away. The 10-inch waves from the Kamchatka quake only removed some materials from the shallow shelf.
L42: Additionally, the timing of this quake is less concerning for the pupfish. With the sun at a high angle in summer, conditions are favorable for algae regrowth. Pupfish typically increase their spawning rates after disturbances, offering hope for a rebound of the Devils Hole Pupfish population.
